      +C\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_\infty\|h\|_2^2.$$ To iterate, apply the same identity to the tensor-valued form $\nabla^j h$. Commuting covariant differentiation with alternating derivative and divergence produces only curvature derivatives multiplied by lower derivatives of $h$. Using [eq:auxiliary-divergence-identities](#eq:auxiliary-divergence-identities), this yields, for fixed $j$, $$\|\nabla^{j+1}h\|_2
  \le C_j\|\phi\|_{H^{j+1}}
      +K_{j,\varepsilon}\|h\|_{H^j},$$ where $K_{j,\varepsilon}$ is a polynomial in finitely many suprema of curvature and its derivatives. Those suprema are polynomially bounded by [lem:auxiliary-geometry](#lem:auxiliary-geometry). Induction starting with [eq:auxiliary-exact-ltwo](#eq:auxiliary-exact-ltwo) thus bounds $\|h\|_{H^k}$ by a polynomial multiple of $\|\phi\|_{H^k}$, without losing derivatives. Finally [eq:auxiliary-selfdual-data](#eq:auxiliary-selfdual-data) and the frame and inverse-Gram bounds give the same estimate in terms of $f$. Smooth approximation, or the fixed-metric Green formula, gives the Sobolev version. Uniqueness is always asserted for $h$, rather than for its one-form primitive. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-51"></a>
#### The nonlinear correction

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-auxiliary-inverse-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-auxiliary-inverse</summary>

*Proof of [thm:auxiliary-solution](#thm:auxiliary-solution).* Fix once and for all an integer $k\ge6$. Every constant and exponent in the following argument uses only finitely many derivatives at this order. Let $\mathcal E^k_\varepsilon$ be the closed subspace of $H^k$ two-forms consisting of exact forms. Equivalently, its elements are distributionally closed and have zero harmonic projection; they possess $H^{k+1}$ primitives for this fixed metric.

Writing $D_\varepsilon=D^0_\varepsilon+h$, the desired equations become the fixed-point equation <a id="eq:auxiliary-contraction-map"></a>$$h=\mathcal T_\varepsilon(h):=
   \mathcal L_\varepsilon
    \left(-A\wedge D^0_\varepsilon,\,
          -C\wedge D^0_\varepsilon,\,
          \frac{A^2-(D^0_\varepsilon)^2-h\wedge h}{2}\right).
  \label{eq:auxiliary-contraction-map}$$ This map is defined on all of $\mathcal E^k_\varepsilon$. Indeed, the first two data have integral zero by [eq:auxiliary-exact-moments](#eq:auxiliary-exact-moments), as does the free term in the third slot. For each exact iterate, including Sobolev iterates, $\int_Xh\wedge h=0$ by approximation and Stokes’ theorem. Thus every iteration satisfies precisely the three mean conditions of [lem:auxiliary-inverse](#lem:auxiliary-inverse).

Let $\delta_\varepsilon=\|\mathcal R_\varepsilon\|_{H^k}$, let $P_\varepsilon$ be an inverse bound from [eq:auxiliary-inverse-bound](#eq:auxiliary-inverse-bound), and let $Q_\varepsilon$ be a multiplication bound from [eq:auxiliary-product](#eq:auxiliary-product). Increasing them if necessary, write <a id="eq:auxiliary-polynomial-losses"></a>$$P_\varepsilon\le C\varepsilon^{-p},\qquad
  Q_\varepsilon\le C\varepsilon^{-q},\qquad
  \delta_\varepsilon\le C\varepsilon^{-s}e^{-c/\varepsilon}.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-polynomial-losses}$$ On the ball of radius $R_\varepsilon=2P_\varepsilon\delta_\varepsilon$ in $\mathcal E^k_\varepsilon$, <a id="eq:auxiliary-ball-bound"></a><a id="eq:auxiliary-lipschitz-bound"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
  \|\mathcal T_\varepsilon(h)\|_{H^k}
  &\le P_\varepsilon\delta_\varepsilon+
          \tfrac12P_\varepsilon Q_\varepsilon R_\varepsilon^2,
     \label{eq:auxiliary-ball-bound}\\
  \|\mathcal T_\varepsilon(h)-\mathcal T_\varepsilon(\widetilde h)\|_{H^k}
  &\le P_\varepsilon Q_\varepsilon R_\varepsilon\,
           \|h-\widetilde h\|_{H^k}.
     \label{eq:auxiliary-lipschitz-bound}
\end{aligned}$$ Choose $\varepsilon$ so small that <a id="eq:auxiliary-smallness"></a>$$2P_\varepsilon^2Q_\varepsilon\delta_\varepsilon<\frac12.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-smallness}$$ This is possible because its left side is at most $C\varepsilon^{-(2p+q+s)}e^{-c/\varepsilon}$, which tends to zero. The ball is invariant and the Lipschitz constant is less than $1/2$. The contraction theorem gives an exact solution with <a id="eq:auxiliary-correction-size"></a>$$\|h\|_{H^k}\le 2P_\varepsilon\delta_\varepsilon.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-correction-size}$$ If the residual is zero, the same conclusion follows directly by taking $h=0$. Polynomial losses can always be absorbed by replacing $c$ with any fixed smaller positive exponent. Thus the correction is exponentially small also in $C^0$, by the polynomial Sobolev embedding bound. The uniformly positive Gram matrix of the approximate triple stays positive, with the same choice of sign. [eq:auxiliary-contraction-map](#eq:auxiliary-contraction-map) gives [eq:auxiliary-exact-equations](#eq:auxiliary-exact-equations) exactly.

We finish by proving spatial smoothness; no simultaneous estimate over infinitely many derivative orders is needed. For the now fixed $\varepsilon$, choose a Coulomb primitive $a\in H^{k+1}$ of $h$, so $\mathrm da=h$ and $\mathrm d^*a=0$. The three equations for $D^0_\varepsilon+\mathrm da$, together with this gauge, form a first-order nonlinear system for the four components of $a$. At the solution the principal symbol of its linearization sends a covector-valued unknown $b$ at a nonzero covector $\xi$ to the three wedge slots of $\xi\wedge b$ against $A,C,D_\varepsilon$, together with $\iota_{\xi^\sharp}b$. If the three wedge slots vanish, $\xi\wedge b$ belongs to the negative-definite wedge-orthogonal complement of the positive three-plane. But $(\xi\wedge b)^2=0$, so $\xi\wedge b=0$. It follows that $b$ is a multiple of $\xi$, and the gauge slot then forces $b=0$. The symbol is square, hence invertible.

Since $k\geq6$ in real dimension four, the initial Sobolev order gives $a\in C^{4,\alpha}$ and at least $C^{3,\alpha}$ coefficients for this elliptic linearization, for some $0<\alpha<1$. Differentiate the system in a smooth coordinate chart. The derivative of $a$ satisfies the linearized elliptic system, with right-hand side involving only smooth background derivatives and already controlled first derivatives of $a$. These coefficients and the right-hand side are $C^{3,\alpha}$, so local first-order elliptic estimates with finitely differentiable coefficients (Taylor, n.d.a, sec. 4, Theorem 4.3) give $\partial a\in C^{4,\alpha}$ and hence $a\in C^{5,\alpha}$. Repeating this argument gives smoothness. All constants in this bootstrap may depend on the fixed $\varepsilon$. The resulting $D_\varepsilon$ is therefore smooth and proves the theorem. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-52"></a>
#### The auxiliary class and a uniform chamber estimate

We now prove [prop:auxiliary-class](#prop:auxiliary-class). The prepared fibration lets us compute the class modulo $\mathbb RF$. The resulting estimate will apply to every later definite pair with the same periods, even when the fibers are no longer complex lines for that pair.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-auxiliary-inverse-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-auxiliary-inverse</summary>

*Proof of [prop:auxiliary-class](#prop:auxiliary-class).* We identify integral curve classes with their Poincaré duals. Choose disjoint closed nodal neighborhoods $N_i$ whose boundaries lie outside all gluing cutoffs, and put $U=X\setminus\bigcup_i\operatorname{int}N_i$. The restriction of $E_\varepsilon$ to $U$ is $D^{\mathrm{sf}}_\varepsilon$. If there is at least one node, $U$ fibers over a compact surface with nonempty boundary, whose second real cohomology is zero. Thus the basic term in [eq:auxiliary-semiflat](#eq:auxiliary-semiflat) is exact on $U$, and <a id="eq:auxiliary-restriction-class"></a>$$|_U
  =r_\varepsilon\bigl(\varepsilon[\Psi]|_U
         -a_\varepsilon[A]|_U-b_\varepsilon[C]|_U\bigr).
  \label{eq:auxiliary-restriction-class}$$ In particular its restriction divided by $\varepsilon$ is bounded.

When there is a node, the kernel of the restriction map $H^2(X;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H^2(U;\mathbb R)$ is exactly $\mathbb RF$. To verify this assertion, excision and Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identify $$H^2(X,U;\mathbb R)
    \simeq\bigoplus_i H^2(N_i,\partial N_i;\mathbb R)
    \simeq\bigoplus_i H_2(N_i;\mathbb R).$$ A one-node neighborhood has the homotopy type of a torus with its primitive vanishing cycle killed, and its second homology is generated by the fiber. Under the map to $H^2(X;\mathbb R)$ these generators give the Poincaré dual fiber classes, all equal to the nonzero class $F$. The long exact sequence of the pair gives the assertion. Hence restriction induces an injective map from $H^2(X;\mathbb R)/\mathbb RF$ onto its image. Its inverse on that finite-dimensional image is bounded. [eq:auxiliary-restriction-class](#eq:auxiliary-restriction-class) proves that the class $[D^0_\varepsilon]$ modulo $\mathbb RF$ is $O(\varepsilon)$.

The nonlinear correction is exact, so $[D_\varepsilon]=[D^0_\varepsilon]\in V$. Choose a fixed linear complement of $\mathbb RF$ in $V$ and use it to lift the quotient class divided by $\varepsilon$ to a bounded vector $u_\varepsilon$. This gives $[D_\varepsilon]=\lambda_\varepsilon F+\varepsilon u_\varepsilon$. Choose any regular fiber outside the gluing region. The original glued form has integral $\varepsilon$ there; the subtracted forms $A,C$ have zero fiber integrals, and the correction is exact. Therefore <a id="eq:auxiliary-fiber-area"></a>$$F=r_\varepsilon\varepsilon,\qquad u_\varepsilon F=r_\varepsilon=1+O(e^{-c/\varepsilon}).
  \label{eq:auxiliary-fiber-area}$$ The square normalization and $F^2=0$ now give <a id="eq:auxiliary-lambda"></a>$$\lambda_\varepsilon
    =\frac{1-\varepsilon^2u_\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon F)}.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-lambda}$$ Boundedness of $u_\varepsilon$ and [eq:auxiliary-fiber-area](#eq:auxiliary-fiber-area) prove [eq:auxiliary-class-expansion](#eq:auxiliary-class-expansion).

If there are no nodal fibers, $\Psi$ is defined on all of $X$ and the basic term in [eq:auxiliary-semiflat](#eq:auxiliary-semiflat) is a multiple of $F$ in cohomology. The form $D^{\mathrm{sf}}_\varepsilon$ already solves the equations, so one takes it for $D_\varepsilon$; the same conclusions follow with $u_\varepsilon=[\Psi]$, $r_\varepsilon=1$, and the coefficient computed by [eq:auxiliary-lambda](#eq:auxiliary-lambda).

It remains to establish the uniform implication. By [cor:curve-signs](#cor:curve-signs), every curve class under consideration with $[D_\varepsilon]d>0$ satisfies $d^2\ge-2$ and the following exhaustive alternatives: either $m=Fd\ne0$ has the same sign as $[B]d$, or $d=cF$ for a nonzero real number $c$. The latter alternative has no sign difficulty, since both $[D_\varepsilon]F$ and $[B]F$ are positive.

Choose a null vector $G_1\in V$ with $FG_1=1$. Such a choice is obtained from any vector pairing to one with $F$ by subtracting half its square times $F$. The orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{span}(F,G_1)$ in the Lorentzian space $V$ is negative definite. Decompose $$d=mG_1+nF+z,\qquad
  u_\varepsilon=\alpha_\varepsilon G_1+\beta_\varepsilon F+w_\varepsilon,$$ where $z,w_\varepsilon$ lie in that complement, and use the Euclidean norm $|z|^2=-z^2$ there. We have $\alpha_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon F\ge a_0$ and uniform bounds for $\alpha_\varepsilon,\beta_\varepsilon,w_\varepsilon$.

Suppose that $m<0$. Integrality of $F$ and $d$ means $m=-a$ for an integer $a\ge1$. The square bound gives <a id="eq:auxiliary-negative-intersection"></a>$$-2an-|z|^2=d^2\ge-2,
  \qquad
  n\le\frac{2-|z|^2}{2a}.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-negative-intersection}$$ Complete the square in the negative-definite component: <a id="eq:auxiliary-completed-square"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
  u_\varepsilon d
   &\le\frac{\alpha_\varepsilon}{a}
      -\frac{\alpha_\varepsilon|z|^2}{2a}
      +|w_\varepsilon||z|+|\beta_\varepsilon|a \notag\\
   &\le\frac{\alpha_\varepsilon}{a}
      +a\left(\frac{|w_\varepsilon|^2}{2\alpha_\varepsilon}
                    +|\beta_\varepsilon|\right)
    \le Ka.
  \label{eq:auxiliary-completed-square}
\end{aligned}$$ The constant $K$ is independent of $a,z,d$, and of the future almost-complex structure. It follows that <a id="eq:auxiliary-chamber-exclusion"></a>$$d
   =-\lambda_\varepsilon a+\varepsilon u_\varepsilon d
   \le a\left(-\frac{c_0}{\varepsilon}+K\varepsilon\right)<0
  \label{eq:auxiliary-chamber-exclusion}$$ whenever $\varepsilon^2<c_0/K$ (with no restriction from this inequality if $K=0$). This contradicts $[D_\varepsilon]d>0$ and excludes every negative integer $m$ simultaneously. The remaining alternative $m>0$ gives $[B]d>0$, proving [eq:auxiliary-uniform-transfer](#eq:auxiliary-uniform-transfer).

Finally, both $[D_\varepsilon]$ and $[B]$ have positive square and pair positively with the same nonzero null vector $F$. In a Lorentzian space the two components of the positive cone are distinguished by the sign of pairing with a fixed nonzero null vector: no positive vector is orthogonal to it. Thus the two classes are in the same component. All restrictions on $\varepsilon$ in this proof depend only on fixed construction data and the original periods. They can therefore be imposed before choosing any later pair deformation. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:endpoint"></a>
### The hyperkähler endpoint

We now use the auxiliary form $D$ to construct the endpoint while the actual triples retain the three original classes. The first Kähler step produces $C_1\in[C]$; the uniform chamber estimate keeps $[B]$ available along the segment from $C$ to $C_1$; and the second Kähler step produces its prescribed endpoint $B_1\in[B]$. We then choose the third form smoothly along that segment with both endpoint values fixed, using [lem:smooth-tamers](#lem:smooth-tamers). We first record the classical class and volume criteria used in the two Kähler steps.

<a id="stmt-lem-endpoint-kahler-class"></a>
<div id="lem:endpoint-kahler-class" class="lemma">

**Lemma 56**. *Let $(X,J)$ be a compact connected complex surface with even first Betti number. Suppose a real $(1,1)$ class $H$ has $H^2>0$ and contains a closed form $\beta$ taming $J$. Then $H$ is a Kähler class. If $\nu$ is a smooth positive four-form with $\int_X\nu=H^2$, there is a Kähler form $\beta_1\in H$ with $\beta_1^2=\nu$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-endpoint-kahler-class"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-endpoint-kahler-class</summary>

*Proof.* The compact-surface Kähler criterion gives a Kähler form $\kappa$ because $b_1$ is even (Buchdahl 1999, Theorem 11) <a id="pm-cite-113"></a>[[Buchdahl1999](#ref-Buchdahl1999)]; see also (Lamari 1999, Corollaire 5.7) <a id="pm-cite-114"></a>[[Lamari1999](#ref-Lamari1999)]. Taming gives $$H\cdot[D]>0
 \quad\text{for every nonzero effective curve }D,
 \qquad H\cdot[\kappa]>0.$$ For the second inequality, pointwise $\beta\kappa=\beta^{1,1}\kappa>0$, since the invariant part of a tamer is positive definite. Together with $H^2>0$, these inequalities are the numerical Kähler-class criterion on a surface (Buchdahl 1999, Corollary 15) <a id="pm-cite-115"></a>[[Buchdahl1999](#ref-Buchdahl1999)]. Equivalently, the segment from $[\kappa]$ to $H$ has positive square and remains positive on every curve, so the component condition in the numerical characterization of the Kähler cone is satisfied (Demailly and Păun 2004, Theorem 0.1) <a id="pm-cite-116"></a>[[DemaillyPaun2004](#ref-DemaillyPaun2004)].

Choose a Kähler representative $\kappa_H\in H$ and set $f=\log(\nu/\kappa_H^2)$. The volume hypothesis says $\int_X e^f\kappa_H^2=\int_X\kappa_H^2$. Yau’s theorem produces a smooth cohomologous Kähler form $\beta_1$ with $\beta_1^2=e^f\kappa_H^2=\nu$ (Yau 1978, sec. 4, Theorem 1) <a id="pm-cite-117"></a>[[Yau1978](#ref-Yau1978)]. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-endpoint-hodge-type"></a>
<div id="lem:endpoint-hodge-type" class="lemma">

**Lemma 57**. *Let $X$ be a compact connected Kähler surface with a nowhere-zero holomorphic two-form $\Omega$. A real degree-two class $H$ is of type $(1,1)$ if and only if it is intersection-orthogonal to $[\Re\Omega]$ and $[\Im\Omega]$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-endpoint-hodge-type"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-endpoint-hodge-type</summary>

*Proof.* Every holomorphic two-form is $f\Omega$ for a global holomorphic function $f$, hence is a constant multiple of $\Omega$. Thus $H^{2,0}(X)=\mathbb C[\Omega]$. The real plane generated by its real and imaginary parts is nondegenerate and positive for the intersection form: their squares are equal and positive and their mixed product vanishes. Hodge decomposition and type considerations make its orthogonal complement exactly $H^{1,1}(X;\mathbb R)$. ◻

</details>

<figure id="fig:endpoint-path">

<figcaption>The final deformation. Solid arrows trace the deformation; dashed arrows indicate auxiliary dependencies. The upper row consists of actual triples in the original classes. The auxiliary form supplies the first integrable pair and the numerical control that keeps $[B]$ available along the moving pair. After both Kähler steps, the tamers $B_{t}$ are chosen with initial value $B$ and final value $B_{1}$.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-endpoint-hodge-type-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-endpoint-hodge-type</summary>

*Proof of [thm:main](#thm:main).* We trace the actual form paths and then construct the endpoint; [fig:endpoint-path](#fig:endpoint-path) summarizes the final stages. All coefficient changes below are constant orthogonal changes, and will be undone at the end.

<a id="pm-h-54"></a>
###### *The prepared pair.*

Choose the primitive null class $F$ of [prop:chamber-class](#prop:chamber-class) and rotate the coefficient basis so that $[B]$ points in the direction of $F^+$ and the pair $[A],[C]$ spans its orthogonal plane in $P$. The rotated initial triple is denoted $(A,C,B)$; its cohomology Gram matrix is still the identity.

<a id="eq:endpoint-periods"></a>
The families result and [prop:nonsplitting](#prop:nonsplitting), [thm:pencil](#thm:pencil) give an exact pair deformation to a torus fibration with the stated standard nodal neighborhoods, keeping $B$ fixed. [prop:regular-preparation](#prop:regular-preparation) then gives a further path of positive closed triples to invariant regular data with the auxiliary form $\Psi$. Both stages preserve the three individual classes and start at the actual representatives supplied by the preceding stage. Retain the notation $(A,C,B)$ for the resulting triple. In particular $$\label{eq:endpoint-periods}
 [A]^2=[C]^2=[B]^2=1,\qquad
 [A][C]=[A][B]=[C][B]=0.$$

<a id="pm-h-55"></a>
###### *The auxiliary solution.*

<a id="eq:endpoint-auxiliary"></a>
Fix a sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ for [thm:auxiliary-solution](#thm:auxiliary-solution), [prop:auxiliary-class](#prop:auxiliary-class), and set $D=D_\epsilon$. The form $D$ is closed and smooth and satisfies $$\label{eq:endpoint-auxiliary}
 AD=CD=0,\qquad D^2=A^2>0.$$ The triple with forms $A,C,D$ is positive. The same choice of $\epsilon$ gives the numerical conclusion of [prop:auxiliary-class](#prop:auxiliary-class) for every later definite pair with the classes $[A],[C]$. These choices precede the Kähler constructions that follow.

<a id="pm-h-56"></a>
###### *The first Kähler step.*

By , $A\pm iD$ is a nowhere-zero holomorphic two-form for an integrable complex structure $I$; choose the sign so that $C$ tames $I$. This is possible by [lem:definite-pair](#lem:definite-pair) and positivity of $(A,D,C)$. [prop:topology](#prop:topology) gives even $b_1$, so the surface is Kähler. The period relations <a href="#eq:endpoint-periods" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-periods">[eq:endpoint-periods]</a> and <a href="#eq:endpoint-auxiliary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-auxiliary">[eq:endpoint-auxiliary]</a> give $[C][A]=[C][D]=0$. Therefore [lem:endpoint-hodge-type](#lem:endpoint-hodge-type) puts $[C]$ in real type $(1,1)$.

<a id="eq:endpoint-first-yau"></a>
Apply [lem:endpoint-kahler-class](#lem:endpoint-kahler-class) with $H=[C]$ and $\nu=A^2$. Its integral condition holds by <a href="#eq:endpoint-periods" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-periods">[eq:endpoint-periods]</a>. We obtain a Kähler representative $C_1\in[C]$ satisfying $$\label{eq:endpoint-first-yau}
 AC_1=DC_1=0,\qquad C_1^2=A^2.$$ Let $C_t=(1-t)C+tC_1$. Both endpoints tame $I$, so the entire segment does. Thus $(A,D,C_t)$ is positive, and $(A,C_t)$ is a definite pair in the original pair classes. Moreover $D$ tames its associated almost-complex structure with the continuously chosen sign. Indeed $D$ is wedge-orthogonal to both pair forms by <a href="#eq:endpoint-auxiliary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-auxiliary">[eq:endpoint-auxiliary]</a> and <a href="#eq:endpoint-first-yau" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-first-yau">[eq:endpoint-first-yau]</a>, and has positive square.

<a id="pm-h-57"></a>
###### *Keeping the third class.*

Let $J_t$ now denote the structure associated with the moving pair $(A,C_t)$ and tamed by $D$. For every irreducible $J_t$ curve, its class $d$ has $[D]d>0$. [prop:auxiliary-class](#prop:auxiliary-class) implies $[B]d>0$, and places $[B]$ and $[D]$ in the same open timelike cone of the fixed space $V$ from <a href="#eq:pair-lorentz-space" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:pair-lorentz-space">[eq:pair-lorentz-space]</a>. The hypotheses of [thm:taming-cone](#thm:taming-cone) therefore hold with $U=[D]$ and $H=[B]$. Thus $[B]$ contains a tamer for every $J_t$.

At $t=0$ this sign of $J_t$ agrees with the sign previously tamed by the actual third form $B$. To check this pointwise, take a regular fiber with its prepared orientation. Both $B$ and $D$ restrict positively to its tangent planes, which are complex lines for the prepared pair. They therefore select the same sign there. On the connected manifold $X$ this choice of sign cannot jump, so $B$ tames $J_0$ everywhere. We will choose the family of tamers after fixing its final representative in the next step.

<a id="pm-h-58"></a>
###### *The second Kähler step.*

<a id="eq:endpoint-final-identities"></a>
The final pair $(A,C_1)$ is orthogonal with equal square by <a href="#eq:endpoint-first-yau" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-first-yau">[eq:endpoint-first-yau]</a>. Thus the structure $J_1$ already selected by $D$ is integrable, with holomorphic volume form $A\pm iC_1$ for the corresponding sign. The preceding step supplies a representative of $[B]$ taming this same $J_1$. Even $b_1$ gives Kählerness again, and <a href="#eq:endpoint-periods" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-periods">[eq:endpoint-periods]</a> together with [lem:endpoint-hodge-type](#lem:endpoint-hodge-type) puts $[B]$ in type $(1,1)$. Apply [lem:endpoint-kahler-class](#lem:endpoint-kahler-class) with $H=[B]$ and $\nu=A^2$. This yields a Kähler representative $B_1\in[B]$ such that $$\label{eq:endpoint-final-identities}
 AB_1=C_1B_1=0,\qquad B_1^2=A^2=C_1^2.$$ Now apply [lem:smooth-tamers](#lem:smooth-tamers) to the family $J_t$, prescribing the actual prepared form $B$ at $t=0$ and the newly constructed $B_1$ at $t=1$. It gives closed tamers $B_t\in[B]$ with these two endpoint values. Thus $(A,C_t,B_t)$ is a path of positive closed triples in the original classes, joining the prepared triple to $(A,C_1,B_1)$ itself.

Concatenate the finitely many triple paths, reparametrizing each to be constant to all orders at its endpoints. This produces a smooth path on $[0,1]$. Each component is closed and remains in its original class, and positivity holds at every parameter. By <a href="#eq:endpoint-first-yau" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-first-yau">[eq:endpoint-first-yau]</a> and <a href="#eq:endpoint-final-identities" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:endpoint-final-identities">[eq:endpoint-final-identities]</a>, if $(\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_3)=(A,C_1,B_1)$ and $\mu_1=A^2/2$, then $$\eta_i\wedge\eta_j=2\delta_{ij}\mu_1.$$ By [lem:complex-symplectic](#lem:complex-symplectic), these forms are parallel and self-dual for a hyperkähler metric with volume $\mu_1$. Finally undo the initial orthogonal change of coefficients. Orthogonality preserves the displayed identity and restores the original ordered classes, proving the theorem. ◻

</details>

      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[\n  box/.style={draw=blue!45!black,rounded corners=2pt,\n    fill=blue!3,align=center,text width=3.35cm,minimum height=1.05cm,\n    inner sep=5pt,font=\\small},\n  aux/.style={box,draw=green!35!black,fill=green!3,text width=4.1cm},\n  route/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]},thick,draw=blue!50!black},\n  aid/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]},dashed,draw=green!35!black},\n  lab/.style={font=\\scriptsize,align=center,fill=white,inner sep=2pt}\n]\n\\node[box] (start) at (0,0) {Prepared triple\\\\$A,C,B$};\n\\node[box] (move) at (4.65,0) {Moving triple\\\\$A,C_t,B_t$};\n\\node[box] (finish) at (9.3,0) {Hyperk\\\"ahler triple\\\\$A,C_1,B_1$};\n\\draw[route] (start) -- node[lab,above=20pt] {$C_t\\in[C]$\\\\$B_t\\in[B]$} (move);\n\\draw[route] (move) -- node[lab,above=20pt] {prescribed\\\\endpoint} (finish);\n\\node[aux] (auxiliary) at (4.65,-2.25)\n  {Auxiliary closed form $D$\\\\$AD=CD=0$,\\quad $D^2=A^2$};\n\\draw[aid] (start.south) -- ++(0,-1.725) --\n  node[lab,below] {small fiber area} (auxiliary.west);\n\\draw[aid] (auxiliary.north) -- node[lab,right]\n  {K\\\"ahler step for $A\\pm iD$\\\\in $[C]$; taming criterion for $[B]$} (move.south);\n\\draw[aid] (auxiliary.east) -- (finish.south |- auxiliary.east) --\n  node[lab,right] {using $C_1$ and\\\\a tamer in $[B]$:\\\\K\\\"ahler step for\\\\$A\\pm iC_1$} (finish.south);\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "Flowchart diagram showing the progression of triples and auxiliary forms:\n- Top row consists of three solid rectangular boxes arranged horizontally:\n  - Left: \"Prepared triple / $A, C, B$\"\n  - Middle: \"Moving triple / $A, C_t, B_t$\"\n  - Right: \"Hyperkähler triple / $A, C_1, B_1$\"\n- A solid horizontal arrow connects \"Prepared triple\" to \"Moving triple\", labeled above with \"$C_t \\in [C]$\" and \"$B_t \\in [B]$\".\n- A solid horizontal arrow connects \"Moving triple\" to \"Hyperkähler triple\", labeled above with \"prescribed endpoint\".\n- Centered below the first transition is a solid rectangular box: \"Auxiliary closed form $D$ / $AD = CD = 0, \\quad D^2 = A^2$\".\n- A dashed arrow points from the auxiliary form box to the \"Prepared triple\" box, labeled \"small fiber area\".\n- A dashed arrow points upward from the auxiliary form box to the arrow between the first two triples, labeled to the right with: \"Kähler step for $A \\pm iD$ / in $[C]$; taming criterion for $[B]$\".\n- Below the second transition is a dashed rectangular box containing: \"using $C_1$ and / a tamer in $[B]$: / Kähler step for / $A \\pm iC_1$\". A dashed arrow points upward from this box to the \"Hyperkähler triple\" box."
    }
